content.text:
**Observations**

- *Which pixels were ever used.* The weights of W1 fall into two populations: values confined to ±0.036 (exactly the PyTorch default init range 1/√784 ≈ 0.0357, i.e. pixels that never received a gradient because they are always 0 in the training data) and clearly trained values up to ±0.38. Mapping the trained rows to image coordinates: row 0 is dead except columns 12–15; row 1 is live from column 4 to 23; rows 2–3 are live from column 2 to ~26; from row 4 onward almost every column from 1 to 27 is live; at the bottom, row 26 is live from column 3 to 25 and row 27 from column 4 to 23. So the data fills the frame almost to all four edges, but the four corners are always empty (a rounded, frame-filling footprint). Content touches the top rows (1–3), the bottom rows (26–27) and the side columns (1–2, 25–27).
- *Where the large weights are.* Very large weights sit (a) along the top rows 1–3, especially at the left/right "shoulder" positions (cols 2–10 and 20–25) with weaker weights in the top centre; (b) along the bottom rows 26–27, with a strong centre block at cols 13–17 and strong corner-ish blocks at cols 3–7 and 20–24; (c) at the left edge, cols 1–5 of rows ~12–16, where three consecutive rows show a near-identical strong sign pattern across all 16 units (−,−,−,+,−,+,+,+,+,−,−,−,+,+,+,+); (d) at the right edge, cols 24–27 of rows ~4–5 and ~24–26. The centre of the image has mostly moderate, smoothly varying weights.
- *Hidden units.* Unit 2 (bias −0.22) is strongly negative for content in rows 1–3 and row 27 and at the left edge, and mildly positive for content in the central columns: it is a "tall object touching top and bottom, hollow/narrow in the middle" detector. Unit 5 is the positive mirror of that for the top rows (+0.2 to +0.38 at rows 1–3). Unit 14 is negative for top-right content and positive for bottom-centre and left-middle content (a "wide, low object" detector). Unit 15 (bias −0.49) is negative for top and bottom content and positive for middle-right content. Units 4, 6, 8, 10 have large positive biases (0.24–0.44), units 2, 12, 14, 15 negative biases, i.e. several units are pushed into one tanh saturation side by default and are flipped by dense inputs.
- *Output layer.* W2 is dense with magnitudes up to 1.5. Unit 2 (negative when top+bottom edges are lit) feeds classes 1 (−0.83) and 3 (−1.10) positively and classes 0, 8, 4 negatively. Unit 14 feeds classes 0, 1, 2, 7 positively and 4, 5 negatively. Output biases: class 5 highest (+0.57), classes 0 and 8 lowest (−0.44, −0.42) — classes with few lit pixels need a positive bias, classes with dense images a negative one.

**Reasoning**

- MNIST, EMNIST, KMNIST, Kannada-MNIST and similar handwritten-character sets place a 20×20 glyph in a 28×28 field with a ~4-pixel margin; their border rows/columns are essentially always zero, so rows 1–3, 26–27 and columns 1–2, 26–27 would all show init-noise weights. Here those rows carry some of the *largest* weights in the network, so centred-glyph datasets are ruled out.
- notMNIST or rendered-font sets would have glyphs filling the corners (E, H, B…) — but all four corners are dead pixels here. Medical/natural 28×28 sets (MedMNIST etc.) have non-zero backgrounds and no dead pixels at all; also they are mostly RGB or not 10-class.
- The footprint — objects scaled so their long axis spans the full 28 pixels, sometimes tall (touching rows 0/1 and 27 in the central columns), sometimes wide (touching columns 1 and 27 in the middle rows), never the corners — is exactly the Fashion-MNIST preprocessing (longest edge resized to 28, centred on the canvas). The discriminative "shoulder" pixels in rows 1–3 at cols 2–10 / 20–25 (shirts/coats vs. trousers/dresses/bags), the left-edge mid-row block (toe of a shoe or bag edge), the bottom-centre block (hem/legs/sole) are the places where clothing silhouettes differ.
- The class semantics line up with the Fashion-MNIST label order: the unit that fires for tall objects touching top and bottom with a hollow centre (unit 2) drives classes 1 and 3 — trouser and dress — and suppresses classes 0 and 8 (T-shirt, bag); the "wide, low, no top-right content" unit 14 helps class 7 (sneaker) and the top-row-only unit 5 suppresses 7 and 9 (sneaker, ankle boot) while helping 0, 2, 6, 8 (tops and bag). The sparsest class in Fashion-MNIST, sandal (5), has the largest output bias; the densest (T-shirt, bag) have the most negative.

**Dataset**

Fashion-MNIST (Zalando article images, 28×28 grayscale, 10 classes).

**Classes**

0 T-shirt/top, 1 Trouser, 2 Pullover, 3 Dress, 4 Coat, 5 Sandal, 6 Shirt, 7 Sneaker, 8 Bag, 9 Ankle boot.

**Confidence**

75%
